metadata.stage: Stage A — Ground Truth Integrity Audit
metadata.oracle_verdict: ORACLE HIGHLY SOUND (Minor Scope Refinements Identified)

corrections.original_statement: Default duration is 2 * MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime), traditionally 60 to 120 seconds
corrections.corrected_statement: RFC 9293 Section 3.3.2 defines MSL as 2 minutes (2*MSL = 240 seconds), though modern OS implementations conventionally configure 60 seconds (Linux TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN) or 120 seconds (BSD).
corrections.reason: Disentangles RFC protocol specification (240s) from operating system implementation conventions (60-120s).

corrections.original_statement: To prevent CRIME/BREACH compression side-channel attacks, sensitive headers (like cookies or authorization) can be flagged Never-Indexed
corrections.corrected_statement: HPACK mitigates compression side-channel attacks (CRIME/BREACH) by providing the Never-Indexed literal representation; implementations MUST explicitly designate sensitive headers (e.g. Cookie, Authorization) as Never-Indexed.
corrections.reason: Clarifies that HPACK provides the protocol mechanism, but active mitigation requires implementation-level header designation.

audited_facts.fact_text: Status code is 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After header indicates how long to wait before making a new request
Retry-After can be specified in seconds or as an HTTP-date
0-RTT Early Data is vulnerable to replay attacks because it lacks forward secrecy before handshake completion
audited_facts.claimed_source: IETF RFC 8446 (The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3)

audited_facts.fact_text: An attacker can intercept and re-transmit 0-RTT request data to the server
audited_facts.claimed_source: IETF RFC 8446 (The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3)

audited_facts.fact_text: Mitigations include single-use tickets, server ticket age verification, client hello recording, or restricting 0-RTT to idempotent requests
audited_facts.claimed_source: IETF RFC 8446 (The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3)

audited_facts.fact_text: Commit object contains a tree pointer (root directory SHA), parent commit SHA(s), author metadata, committer metadata, and commit message
Historically hashed with SHA-1 (160-bit), modern Git supports SHA-256 (256-bit)
Forms an immutable directed acyclic graph (Merkle DAG)
TIME_WAIT ensures the remote endpoint has received the final ACK closing the connection
Prevents delayed duplicate segments from an old connection from interfering with a new incarnation on the same 4-tuple
Default duration is 2 * MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime), traditionally 60 to 120 seconds
audited_facts.auditor_notes: RFC 9293 Section 3.3.2 specifies MSL = 2 minutes (2MSL = 240s). The 60-120s duration is an OS implementation convention (e.g. Linux TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN = 60s), not the RFC default.

audited_facts.fact_text: WAL records all changes to disk before data pages are updated in shared buffers, providing ACID durability
audited_facts.claimed_source: PostgreSQL Documentation (Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log)

audited_facts.fact_text: Checkpoints periodically flush all dirty data pages from shared buffers to disk and write a checkpoint record to WAL
audited_facts.claimed_source: PostgreSQL Documentation (Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log)

audited_facts.fact_text: During crash recovery, replay only needs to start from the last checkpoint REDO record rather than the beginning of WAL
audited_facts.claimed_source: PostgreSQL Documentation (Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log)

audited_facts.fact_text: Split votes happen when multiple followers become candidates simultaneously and divide votes equally
audited_facts.claimed_source: Ongaro & Ousterhout (In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, USENIX ATC 2014)

audited_facts.fact_text: Raft uses randomized election timeouts (typically 150-300ms) to break the symmetry
audited_facts.claimed_source: Ongaro & Ousterhout (In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, USENIX ATC 2014)

audited_facts.fact_text: The candidate with the shortest timeout will time out first, increment the term, and request votes before others
audited_facts.claimed_source: Ongaro & Ousterhout (In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, USENIX ATC 2014)

audited_facts.fact_text: HPACK maintains a static table of 61 common header fields and an evicting dynamic table of negotiated header fields
audited_facts.claimed_source: IETF RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)

audited_facts.fact_text: Header values can be encoded with static Huffman coding
audited_facts.claimed_source: IETF RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)

audited_facts.fact_text: To prevent CRIME/BREACH compression side-channel attacks, sensitive headers (like cookies or authorization) can be flagged Never-Indexed
audited_facts.claimed_source: IETF RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)
audited_facts.auditor_notes: HPACK provides the Never-Indexed representation mechanism, but mitigation of CRIME/BREACH requires explicit application/implementation designation of sensitive headers.

audited_facts.fact_text: Hashes stream items and observes the maximum number of leading zeros in the hash suffix across m registers
audited_facts.claimed_source: Flajolet et al. (HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm, 2007)

audited_facts.fact_text: Uses the harmonic mean of 2^(leading zeros) across registers to reduce susceptibility to outliers
audited_facts.claimed_source: Flajolet et al. (HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm, 2007)

audited_facts.fact_text: Standard error is approximately 1.04 / sqrt(m), requiring minimal memory (e.g. 12 KB for 16,384 registers in Redis)
audited_facts.claimed_source: Flajolet et al. (HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm, 2007)

audited_facts.fact_text: Write amplification measures physical bytes written to storage per logical byte updated
Size-Tiered compaction optimizes for low write amplification but suffers from high space amplification (up to 100%) and higher read amplification
Leveled compaction bounds space amplification (typically ~10%) and reduces read amplification by guaranteeing at most one SST per key per level, but incurs higher write amplification
Performs static control-flow graph (CFG) analysis to verify that program is a DAG with bounded execution (no infinite loops)
Simulates instruction execution to track register state, value ranges, and types (scalar vs pointer)
Enforces bounds checking on all pointer dereferences to prevent out-of-bounds kernel memory reads/writes
Prohibits uninitialized memory access and guarantees program termination
In 2PC, if the coordinator crashes after participants have voted YES (prepared) but before sending COMMIT, participants must wait indefinitely holding resource locks
3PC splits the commit decision into PreCommit, ensuring that participants never commit until all participants have acknowledged prepare
3PC allows operational participants to elect a new coordinator and safely timeout to abort or commit without blocking under crash-stop assumptions
Traditional read/write requires copying data from kernel page cache to user-space buffer and back to socket kernel buffer (4 context switches, 4 data copies)
sendfile() transfers data directly from page cache to the target socket file descriptor within kernel space
With DMA scatter-gather hardware support, data is transferred directly from page cache to network interface without CPU copying
HNSW constructs a multi-layer proximity graph offering state-of-the-art query recall and low query latency, but requires substantial RAM to store raw vectors and graph edges
audited_facts.claimed_source: Malkov & Yashunin (HNSW 2018) / Jegou et al. (Product Quantization 2011)

audited_facts.fact_text: IVF-PQ clusters the vector space with inverted lists (IVF) and compresses vectors into compact byte codes via Product Quantization (PQ)
audited_facts.claimed_source: Malkov & Yashunin (HNSW 2018) / Jegou et al. (Product Quantization 2011)

audited_facts.fact_text: IVF-PQ reduces memory footprint by 8x-32x and supports massive billions-scale datasets, at the cost of lower recall and training overhead
audited_facts.claimed_source: Malkov & Yashunin (HNSW 2018) / Jegou et al. (Product Quantization 2011)

audited_facts.fact_text: In basic consistent hashing, non-uniform random placement of nodes on the hash ring causes high variance in partition range sizes
audited_facts.claimed_source: Karger et al. (Consistent Hashing 1997) / DeCandia et al. (Dynamo 2007)

audited_facts.fact_text: Virtual nodes (vnodes) assign each physical node multiple distinct positions (e.g. 128-256 tokens) across the ring
audited_facts.claimed_source: Karger et al. (Consistent Hashing 1997) / DeCandia et al. (Dynamo 2007)

audited_facts.fact_text: When a node joins or leaves, the load is uniformly distributed across all remaining nodes rather than overwhelming the immediate successor
audited_facts.claimed_source: Karger et al. (Consistent Hashing 1997) / DeCandia et al. (Dynamo 2007)

audited_facts.fact_text: Phase 1a (Prepare): Proposer selects proposal number n and sends Prepare(n) to a majority of acceptors
audited_facts.claimed_source: Lamport (The Part-Time Parliament 1998 / Paxos Made Simple 2001)

audited_facts.fact_text: Phase 1b (Promise): Acceptors promise not to accept any future proposals numbered < n, returning the highest-numbered proposal already accepted (if any)
audited_facts.claimed_source: Lamport (The Part-Time Parliament 1998 / Paxos Made Simple 2001)

audited_facts.fact_text: Phase 2a (Accept): Proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value of the highest-numbered proposal in promises or a new value
audited_facts.claimed_source: Lamport (The Part-Time Parliament 1998 / Paxos Made Simple 2001)

audited_facts.fact_text: Phase 2b (Accepted): Acceptors accept the proposal unless they have already promised a higher proposal number
audited_facts.claimed_source: Lamport (The Part-Time Parliament 1998 / Paxos Made Simple 2001)

audited_facts.fact_text: vm.overcommit_memory=0 uses heuristic overcommit algorithm (default)
vm.overcommit_memory=1 always allows overcommit without checking available memory
vm.overcommit_memory=2 enforces strict limit: CommitLimit = Swap + (RAM * overcommit_ratio)
OOM killer computes oom_score based on percentage of RAM/swap consumed, adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 to +1000)
gRPC utilizes binary Protocol Buffers encoding, reducing serialization overhead and payload size compared to textual JSON
audited_facts.claimed_source: gRPC / Protocol Buffers & HTTP/2 Architecture Specs

audited_facts.fact_text: gRPC runs natively over HTTP/2 providing connection multiplexing, flow control, and full duplex bidirectional streaming
audited_facts.claimed_source: gRPC / Protocol Buffers & HTTP/2 Architecture Specs

audited_facts.fact_text: REST over HTTP/1.1 requires separate connections or head-of-line blocking, but offers ubiquitous browser compatibility and human-readable debugging
audited_facts.claimed_source: gRPC / Protocol Buffers & HTTP/2 Architecture Specs

audited_facts.fact_text: Flink is a native pipelined event-at-a-time streaming engine with sub-second latencies (milliseconds)
audited_facts.claimed_source: Apache Flink & Apache Spark Official Documentation

audited_facts.fact_text: Spark Structured Streaming is historically micro-batch driven, providing high throughput for analytics at slightly higher latency (tens to hundreds of ms)
audited_facts.claimed_source: Apache Flink & Apache Spark Official Documentation

audited_facts.fact_text: Flink uses Chandy-Lamport distributed asynchronous checkpointing for exact once state, whereas Spark relies on write-ahead logs and RDD lineage replay
audited_facts.claimed_source: Apache Flink & Apache Spark Official Documentation

audited_facts.fact_text: Rollback journal locks the entire database exclusively during writes, completely blocking concurrent readers
WAL mode appends changes to a separate -wal file, allowing multiple concurrent readers to read unaffected database pages while a writer writes
WAL requires periodic checkpointing and shared memory (-shm file), and does not work over networked filesystems (NFS/CIFS)
ClickHouse is an open-source columnar DBMS optimized for ultra-high ingest rates (millions of rows/sec) and real-time low-latency analytical aggregations on bare-metal or cloud
Snowflake is a fully managed cloud data warehouse featuring decoupled compute and cloud storage (S3/GCS/Blob)
ClickHouse excels at sub-second telemetry and clickstream dashboards; Snowflake excels at multi-departmental BI, semi-structured queries, and elastic auto-scaling
NGINX is a high-performance event-driven web server and reverse proxy with traditional static configuration files or commercial reload APIs
Envoy is designed from inception as a service mesh sidecar proxy with dynamic control plane APIs (xDS for listeners, routes, clusters, endpoints)
Envoy provides native out-of-the-box support for distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), gRPC transcoding, and L7 filter pipelines
Cap'n Proto formats data in memory identically to its wire format, completely eliminating the encode/decode step (true zero-copy)
audited_facts.claimed_source: Cap'n Proto & Protocol Buffers Technical Documentation

audited_facts.fact_text: Protocol Buffers encodes values with variable-length integers (varints) and nested tags, requiring CPU cycles to pack and parse into language objects
audited_facts.claimed_source: Cap'n Proto & Protocol Buffers Technical Documentation

audited_facts.fact_text: Cap'n Proto trades slightly larger wire payload sizes for zero-CPU serialization and sub-microsecond IPC latency
audited_facts.claimed_source: Cap'n Proto & Protocol Buffers Technical Documentation

audited_facts.fact_text: CockroachDB implements Multi-Raft across range partitions, embeds the storage engine (Pebble) in every node, and uses the PostgreSQL wire protocol
TiDB separates compute (TiDB stateless SQL servers) from storage (TiKV distributed transactional key-value cluster running Raft), using MySQL wire protocol
Both provide serializable/snapshot isolation and automatic range splitting, but differ in compute/storage decoupling and protocol compatibility
Prometheus uses a pull model where the server periodically scrapes /metrics HTTP endpoints discovered via service discovery (Kubernetes/Consul)
InfluxDB uses a push model where applications or edge agents (Telegraf) stream metrics directly over HTTP/UDP to the database
Pull models simplify target health monitoring and prevent server overload; push models handle short-lived batch jobs and ephemeral serverless functions more naturally
Total Savings = Annual Savings * Years; Net Profit = Total Savings - Upfront Cost; ROI = (Net Profit / Upfront Cost) * 100
audited_facts.auditor_notes: Independently computed and mathematically exact from first principles.

audited_facts.fact_text: Speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + (p / N))
audited_facts.auditor_notes: Independently computed and mathematically exact from first principles.

audited_facts.fact_text: BDP_bytes = Bandwidth (bits/sec) * RTT (sec) / 8; BDP_MB = BDP_bytes / 10^6 (or / 1024^2)
audited_facts.auditor_notes: Independently computed and mathematically exact from first principles.

audited_facts.fact_text: Total FLOPs = 6 * Parameters * Tokens
audited_facts.auditor_notes: Independently computed and mathematically exact from first principles.

audited_facts.fact_text: Ending ARR = Starting ARR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn; NRR = (Ending ARR / Starting ARR) * 100
audited_facts.auditor_notes: Independently computed and mathematically exact from first principles.

audited_facts.fact_text: Record Size = Payload + Overhead; Unreplicated Bytes = Records * Record Size; Total Replicated Bytes = Unreplicated Bytes * 3; Storage GB = Replicated Bytes / 10^9 (or 1024^3)
audited_facts.auditor_notes: Independently computed and mathematically exact from first principles.
